message: Math.round(x * 100) hardcodes two decimals: it charges 100x in the 16 zero-decimal currencies (JPY, KRW, VND, XOF, CLP and the rest) and 10x too little in the 3-decimal ones (KWD, BHD, JOD, OMR, TND). Scale by the currency's ISO 4217 exponent.
The amount field is built with * 100. Payment APIs take an integer of the currency's minor unit, and that unit is not 1/100 for every currency.
toFixed(2) prints 1200.00 for JPY, which has no minor unit at all, and truncates KWD 1.234 to 1.23 - a real 0.004 KWD error on every line. Format with Intl.NumberFormat and the ISO code.
amount is a decimal literal. The API expects an integer of minor units, so 10.99 is read as 10 or rejected outright.
parseFloat on money gives a binary float: 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004. Carry money as an integer of minor units, never as a float.
BGN: Bulgaria adopted the euro on 2026-01-01 and the lev stopped being legal tender on 2026-02-01. Charge "eur" - the fixed conversion was 1 EUR = 1.95583 BGN.
BGN: Bulgaria adopted the euro on 2026-01-01 and the lev stopped being legal tender on 2026-02-01. Charge EUR - the fixed conversion was 1 EUR = 1.95583 BGN.
HRK was withdrawn when Croatia adopted the euro on 2023-01-01. Charge "eur" - the fixed conversion was 1 EUR = 7.53450 HRK.
HRK was withdrawn when Croatia adopted the euro on 2023-01-01. Charge EUR - the fixed conversion was 1 EUR = 7.53450 HRK.
Retired ISO 4217 code. VEF is now VES, MRO is MRU, STD is STN, SLL is SLE, ZWL is ZWG, and LTL, EEK and SKK were replaced by EUR. A retired code is rejected, so the charge never happens.
ISK and UGX are zero-decimal, but payment APIs still expect a two-decimal value whose last two digits are 00 - 5 ISK is amount 500. Sending 5 undercharges by 100x.
3-decimal currency (ISO 4217 exponent 3). The amount is in thousandths and the last digit must be 0: KWD 1.5 is 1500, not 150.
Zero-decimal currency: the amount IS the charge. 500 JPY is amount 500, so any multiplication by 100 on this line charges 100x.
HUF and TWD are charged with two decimals but paid out as zero-decimal: a manual payout amount must be evenly divisible by 100, so a balance of 1045 cannot be paid out in full.
'$' + amount hardcodes the symbol and the en-US grouping. The same value must read 1.234,56 with the symbol after the number in de-DE. Use Intl.NumberFormat(locale, {style:'currency', currency}).
Intl.NumberFormat with style 'currency' and no currency option throws a TypeError at runtime, not at build time.
Math.round on a float tax amount rounds 1.005 down to 1, because 1.005 is stored as 1.00499999999999989. Round on integer minor units instead.
A hardcoded FX rate. Only the euro conversion rates are legally fixed (1 EUR = 1.95583 BGN and 7.53450 HRK); every other rate moves daily.
A variable named for minor units is holding a decimal. Minor units are whole numbers by definition, so this value is already wrong before it is sent.
Comparing a money float for equality. 0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3 is false in every IEEE-754 language, so this branch silently never runs.
parseInt(x.toFixed(...)) truncates at the first non-digit, so 1.99 becomes 1 - the decimal part is dropped, not scaled.
Dividing by 100 to display an amount assumes two decimals. For JPY it divides the charge by 100; for KWD it leaves the last digit in the wrong place.
toLocaleString() with no arguments formats with the machine's locale, so a server in Frankfurt prints a different number than a laptop in Chicago.
Number() on a money string produces a float, the same trap as parseFloat: the value can no longer be summed or compared exactly.
